title: 1 Chronicles 19:10–19
context: Caught between the Ammonites and the Syrians, Joab divides his forces with his brother Abishai, encourages them to be strong for their people and the cities of God, and commits the outcome to the LORD. Both enemy forces flee. When the Syrians regroup with forces from beyond the River under Shophach, David leads Israel and defeats them, and Hadadezer's servants make peace and serve him. This parallels 2 Samuel 10:9–19, with some differences in figures and spelling.

verses.text: Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose some of all the choice men of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab sees the battle set "before and behind" and chooses his best men to face the Syrians. Arminian readers note Joab's wise and responsible leadership in a dangerous situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:9. Faced with enemies on two fronts, Joab acts with skill, yet the following verses show that he places the outcome in God's hands.

verses.text: The rest of the people he committed into the hand of Abishai his brother; and they put themselves in array against the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: He gives the rest of the army to Abishai to face the Ammonites. Arminian readers note the trust placed in Abishai and the shared responsibility in the battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:10. The brothers' cooperation shows the value of mutual support among God's people when they face danger together.

verses.text: He said, “If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you are to help me; but if the children of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will help you.
verses.arminianNotes: "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you are to help me." Arminian readers see a plan of mutual aid, a practical picture of how God's people should support one another in conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:11. Joab's plan is sound military strategy, but it is only the first half of his speech; the second half turns to God.

verses.text: Be courageous, and let’s be strong for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do that which seems good to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joab urges, "Be courageous," and then prays, "May the LORD do that which seems good to him." Arminian readers see courage and responsible action joined with humble trust, as Joab does his part and leaves the result to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joab's words, paralleled in 2 Samuel 10:12, confess that the outcome belongs to God's good pleasure. Human effort and divine sovereignty stand together without tension here.

verses.text: So Joab and the people who were with him came near to the front of the Syrians to the battle; and they fled before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab advances against the Syrians, and they flee. Arminian readers note that the hired army, fighting without real stake in the cause, gives way before Israel's determined advance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:13. The rapid flight of the Syrians shows that God answered Joab's trust by giving Israel the victory.

verses.text: When the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The Ammonites flee into the city, and Joab returns to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the immediate threat is ended, though Ammon itself is not yet subdued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:14. The unfinished campaign against Ammon's city sets up the siege of Rabbah in chapter 20.

verses.text: When the Syrians saw that they were defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and called out the Syrians who were beyond the River, with Shophach the captain of the army of Hadadezer leading them.
verses.arminianNotes: The defeated Syrians call forces from beyond the River under Shophach, Hadadezer's commander. Arminian readers note that the Syrians choose to renew the conflict rather than accept defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 10:16 spells the commander's name Shobach and names Helam as the meeting place. The Chronicler's form is recorded without resolving the difference.

verses.text: David was told that, so he gathered all Israel together, passed over the Jordan, came to them, and set the battle in array against them. So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him.
verses.arminianNotes: David gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan, and engages the Syrians. Arminian readers note that David himself now leads the army, taking responsibility as Israel's king in the decisive battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:17. The Chronicler emphasizes "all Israel" gathered under David, a theme that runs through his presentation of David's reign.

verses.text: The Syrians fled before Israel; and David killed of the Syrian men seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand footmen, and also killed Shophach the captain of the army.
verses.arminianNotes: David kills seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand footmen, and Shophach. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 10:18 gives seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen; the accounts differ, and these notes leave that difference standing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note, consistent with the notes on 2 Samuel 10:18, that both accounts describe the same decisive victory and the death of Hadadezer's commander. The figures differ and are not harmonized here.

verses.text: When the servants of Hadadezer saw that they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and served him. The Syrians would not help the children of Ammon any more.
verses.arminianNotes: Hadadezer's servants make peace with David and serve him, and the Syrians will no longer help Ammon. Arminian readers see the fruit of victory: peace with former enemies and the isolation of Ammon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:19, which speaks of "all the kings who were servants to Hadadezer." God's establishment of David's kingdom brings surrounding nations into submission.
